839.54: whether in those countries I had travelled, as well as my own, I had not observed the same general disposition.” After this pre
839.55: face, he gave me a particular account of the _struldbrugs_ among them. He said, “they commonly acted like mortals till about thi
839.56: rty years old; after which, by degrees, they grew melancholy and dejected, increasing in both till they came to fourscore. This
839.57: he learned from their own confession: for otherwise, there not being above two or three of that species born in an age, they wer
839.58: e too few to form a general observation by. When they came to fourscore years, which is reckoned the extremity of living in this
839.59: country, they had not only all the follies and infirmities of other old men, but many more which arose from the dreadful prospe
839.60: ct of never dying. They were not only opinionative, peevish, covetous, morose, vain, talkative, but incapable of friendship, and
839.61: dead to all natural affection, which never descended below their grandchildren. Envy and impotent desires are their prevailing
839.62: passions. But those objects against which their envy seems principally directed, are the vices of the younger sort and the death
839.63: s of the old. By reflecting on the former, they find themselves cut off from all possibility of pleasure; and whenever they see
839.64: a funeral, they lament and repine that others have gone to a harbour of rest to which they themselves never can hope to arrive.

840.1: They have no remembrance of anything but what they learned and observed in their youth and middleage, and even that is very impe
840.2: rfect; and for the truth or particulars of any fact, it is safer to depend on common tradition, than upon their best recollectio
840.3: ns. The least miserable among them appear to be those who turn to dotage, and entirely lose their memories; these meet with more
840.4: pity and assistance, because they want many bad qualities which abound in others. “If a _struldbrug_ happen to marry one of his
840.5: own kind, the marriage is dissolved of course, by the courtesy of the kingdom, as soon as the younger of the two comes to be fo
840.6: urscore; for the law thinks it a reasonable indulgence, that those who are condemned, without any fault of their own, to a perpe
840.7: tual continuance in the world, should not have their misery doubled by the load of a wife. “As soon as they have completed the t
840.8: erm of eighty years, they are looked on as dead in law; their heirs immediately succeed to their estates; only a small pittance
840.9: is reserved for their support; and the poor ones are maintained at the public charge. After that period, they are held incapable
840.10: of any employment of trust or profit; they cannot purchase lands, or take leases; neither are they allowed to be witnesses in a
840.11: ny cause, either civil or criminal, not even for the decision of meers and bounds. “At ninety, they lose their teeth and hair; t
840.12: hey have at that age no distinction of taste, but eat and drink whatever they can get, without relish or appetite. The diseases
840.13: they were subject to still continue, without increasing or diminishing. In talking, they forget the common appellation of things
840.14: , and the names of persons, even of those who are their nearest friends and relations. For the same reason, they never can amuse
840.15: themselves with reading, because their memory will not serve to carry them from the beginning of a sentence to the end; and by
840.16: this defect, they are deprived of the only entertainment whereof they might otherwise be capable. “The language of this country
840.17: being always upon the flux, the _struldbrugs_ of one age do not understand those of another; neither are they able, after two hu
840.18: ndred years, to hold any conversation (farther than by a few general words) with their neighbours the mortals; and thus they lie
840.19: under the disadvantage of living like foreigners in their own country.” This was the account given me of the _struldbrugs_, as
840.20: near as I can remember. I afterwards saw five or six of different ages, the youngest not above two hundred years old, who were b
840.21: rought to me at several times by some of my friends; but although they were told, “that I was a great traveller, and had seen al
840.22: l the world,” they had not the least curiosity to ask me a question; only desired “I would give them _slumskudask_,” or a token
840.23: of remembrance; which is a modest way of begging, to avoid the law, that strictly forbids it, because they are provided for by t
840.24: he public, although indeed with a very scanty allowance. They are despised and hated by all sorts of people. When one of them is
840.25: born, it is reckoned ominous, and their birth is recorded very particularly so that you may know their age by consulting the re
840.26: gister, which, however, has not been kept above a thousand years past, or at least has been destroyed by time or public disturba
840.27: nces. But the usual way of computing how old they are, is by asking them what kings or great persons they can remember, and then
840.28: consulting history; for infallibly the last prince in their mind did not begin his reign after they were fourscore years old. T
840.29: hey were the most mortifying sight I ever beheld; and the women more horrible than the men. Besides the usual deformities in ext
840.30: reme old age, they acquired an additional ghastliness, in proportion to their number of years, which is not to be described; and
840.31: among half a dozen, I soon distinguished which was the eldest, although there was not above a century or two between them. The
840.32: reader will easily believe, that from what I had heard and seen, my keen appetite for perpetuity of life was much abated. I grew

840.34: th pleasure, from such a life. The king heard of all that had passed between me and my friends upon this occasion, and rallied m
840.35: e very pleasantly; wishing I could send a couple of _struldbrugs_ to my own country, to arm our people against the fear of death

841.24: t trampled on the crucifix;” but the other, who had received instructions to let me pass, gave the rascal twenty strokes on the

841.26: e. We sailed with a fair wind to the Cape of Good Hope, where we staid only to take in fresh water. On the 10th of April, 1710,

841.28: o the sea, not far from the coast of Guinea. From Amsterdam I soon after set sail for England, in a small vessel belonging to th
841.29: at city. On the 16th of April, 1710, we put in at the Downs. I landed next morning, and saw once more my native country, after a

841.49: only fastening one of my legs with a chain, near my bed, and placed a sentry at my door with his piece charged, who was commande
841.50: d to shoot me dead if I attempted my liberty. They sent me down victuals and drink, and took the government of the ship to thems
841.51: elves. Their design was to turn pirates, and plunder the Spaniards, which they could not do till they got more men. But first th
841.52: ey resolved to sell the goods in the ship, and then go to Madagascar for recruits, several among them having died since my confi
841.53: nement. They sailed many weeks, and traded with the Indians; but I knew not what course they took, being kept a close prisoner i

841.57: t of clothes, which were as good as new, and take a small bundle of linen, but no arms, except my hanger; and they were so civil
841.58: as not to search my pockets, into which I conveyed what money I had, with some other little necessaries. They rowed about a lea

841.60: self;” but said, “that the captain” (as they called him) “was resolved, after they had sold the lading, to get rid of me in the
841.61: first place where they could discover land.” They pushed off immediately, advising me to make haste for fear of being overtaken
841.62: by the tide, and so bade me farewell. In this desolate condition I advanced forward, and soon got upon firm ground, where I sat
841.63: down on a bank to rest myself, and consider what I had best do. When I was a little refreshed, I went up into the country, resol
841.64: ving to deliver myself to the first savages I should meet, and purchase my life from them by some bracelets, glass rings, and ot

842.1: her toys, which sailors usually provide themselves with in those voyages, and whereof I had some about me. The land was divided

842.4: l into a beaten road, where I saw many tracts of human feet, and some of cows, but most of horses. At last I beheld several anim

842.7: gave me an opportunity of distinctly marking their form. Their heads and breasts were covered with a thick hair, some frizzled,
842.8: and others lank; they had beards like goats, and a long ridge of hair down their backs, and the fore parts of their legs and fe
842.9: et; but the rest of their bodies was bare, so that I might see their skins, which were of a brown buff colour. They had no tails
842.10: , nor any hair at all on their buttocks, except about the anus, which, I presume, nature had placed there to defend them as they

842.12: es as nimbly as a squirrel, for they had strong extended claws before and behind, terminating in sharp points, and hooked. They

842.14: hair on their heads, but none on their faces, nor any thing more than a sort of down on the rest of their bodies, except about

842.18: ontempt and aversion, I got up, and pursued the beaten road, hoping it might direct me to the cabin of some Indian. I had not go
842.19: t far, when I met one of these creatures full in my way, and coming up directly to me. The ugly monster, when he saw me, distort
842.20: ed several ways, every feature of his visage, and stared, as at an object he had never seen before; then approaching nearer, lif
842.21: ted up his forepaw, whether out of curiosity or mischief I could not tell; but I drew my hanger, and gave him a good blow with t

842.28: midst of this distress, I observed them all to run away on a sudden as fast as they could; at which I ventured to leave the tree
842.29: and pursue the road, wondering what it was that could put them into this fright. But looking on my left hand, I saw a horse wal
842.30: king softly in the field; which my persecutors having sooner discovered, was the cause of their flight. The horse started a litt
842.31: le, when he came near me, but soon recovering himself, looked full in my face with manifest tokens of wonder; he viewed my hands
842.32: and feet, walking round me several times. I would have pursued my journey, but he placed himself directly in the way, yet looki

842.38: er horse came up; who applying himself to the first in a very formal manner, they gently struck each other’s right hoof before,

842.47: ealing my fear as much as I could, for I began to be in some pain how this adventure might terminate; and the reader will easily
